title: Why choice makes us dizzy
text: Kierkegaard compared anxiety to standing at a cliff edge. The dizziness is partly knowing you could jump. For him, anxiety is what freedom feels like from the inside.
author: Søren Kierkegaard
more:
Søren Kierkegaard, a 19th-century Danish thinker often called the first existentialist, published much of his work under made-up names. In The Concept of Anxiety (1844) he separates fear, which has an object, from anxiety, which is about possibility itself. On a height you feel dizzy partly because nothing is stopping you.

The thinkers in this thread all start from the same place. Being human means facing choices no rulebook can settle for you.

text: If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Missiles 12 (trans. Anthony M. Ludovici, 1911)
more:
Nietzsche wrote this in 1888, in a run of short, punchy aphorisms. It got famous in the 20th century when the psychiatrist Viktor Frankl, a Holocaust survivor, quoted a version of it in Man’s Search for Meaning to explain how some prisoners found the strength to endure.

Nietzsche matters to existentialism because he argued the old sources of meaning were fading, and people would have to make their own values. A ‘wherefore’ gives freedom a direction.

title: Nobody is born a coward
text: A paper knife is designed before it’s made. Sartre said people are the reverse: we exist first, with no built-in purpose, then define ourselves by what we do.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
more:
Jean-Paul Sartre gave this lecture in Paris in 1945, and it became the best-known summary of existentialism. His slogan was ‘existence precedes essence’. With no creator designing human nature in advance, there’s no blueprint to check. Nobody is born a coward or a hero.

So ‘that’s just how I am’ never fully works as an excuse. Sartre added that choosing for yourself also sketches what you think a person should be.

title: The waiter who plays a waiter
text: Sartre describes a café waiter who moves a little too precisely, as if acting the part. That’s bad faith, hiding from your freedom behind a role.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
more:
If we make ourselves, why do so few people feel free? Sartre’s answer was bad faith, a self-deception where we hide from our own freedom. The waiter treats ‘waiter’ as his whole essence. The rest of us say ‘I’m just not a creative person’ or ‘my job made me do it’.

Sartre wasn’t mocking waiters, or roles in general. His target was pretending the role does the choosing for you. Bad faith’s favourite line is ‘I had no choice’.

title: My freedom needs yours
text: Simone de Beauvoir argued that if freedom gives life its value, you can’t want it only for yourself. To will yourself free is also to will others free.
author: Simone de Beauvoir
more:
Beauvoir wrote The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947) partly to answer a common attack: if there are no fixed values, isn’t everything permitted? She said no. We’re ambiguous creatures, free but tied to bodies, history and other people, and real freedom only grows where others are free too.

Two years later The Second Sex applied this to women, showing how society had cast them as a fixed ‘other’ instead of free subjects.

title: Sisyphus, smiling
text: The gods sentenced Sisyphus to roll a boulder uphill forever. It always rolls back. Camus saw us in him, then asked us to picture Sisyphus happy.
author: Albert Camus
more:
Camus called the clash between our hunger for meaning and the world’s silence ‘the absurd’. He asked whether it makes life not worth living, and answered no. You live with it, eyes open. He called that response revolt.

Sisyphus is his hero because he knows exactly how hopeless his task is and keeps pushing, owning every step. Camus rejected the existentialist label. Where Sartre says we create meaning, Camus says we can live fully even without it.

title: Choices you pretend aren’t choices
text: Name one thing in your life you call ‘just how it is’. What if it’s a choice you keep making every day?
source: Drawing on Sartre, Being and Nothingness (1943), and Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942)
more:
The thinkers in this thread would say it often is, at least in part. Kierkegaard said freedom makes us dizzy. Nietzsche said we need a why. Sartre said there’s no fixed human nature and we hide from that in bad faith. Beauvoir said real freedom includes other people’s. Camus said we can live fully without answers from the universe.

None of them claimed every circumstance is chosen. Illness, poverty and other people’s actions are real limits.

text: …daily to discourse about virtue … is the greatest good of man, and that the unexamined life is not worth living…
author: Socrates (as written by Plato)
more:
Socrates said this at his trial in Athens in 399 BC, after the jury found him guilty of impiety and corrupting the young. Instead of begging for mercy, he explained that he couldn’t stop questioning people.

‘Examined’ here means tested in conversation. What do you believe about justice or courage, and does it hold up when someone pushes? The jury sentenced him to death.

text: …men come to be builders, for instance, by building … by doing just actions we come to be just … and by doing brave actions brave.
author: Aristotle
source: Nicomachean Ethics, Book 2.1 (trans. D. P. Chase)
more:
Aristotle treats character like a craft. Nobody becomes a harpist by reading about harps, and nobody becomes brave by admiring bravery. You become what you do over and over.

That was a quietly radical idea. It makes virtue a skill rather than a gift you either have or lack. It starts clumsy and turns into second nature with practice.

text: …all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
em: stay quietly in their own chamber
author: Blaise Pascal
more:
Blaise Pascal was a mathematician and inventor who, late in life, gathered notes for a defence of Christianity. He died in 1662 before finishing it, and the fragments came out as the Pensées, or ‘thoughts’. This one is from a section on diversion.

Pascal saw people chase games, wars and busyness mostly to avoid sitting alone with their thoughts. In a 2014 study, many participants chose to give themselves a mild electric shock rather than sit alone with nothing to do for a few minutes.

text: When I play with my cat who knows whether I do not make her more sport than she makes me?
em: more sport than she makes me
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Essays, Book 2.12, Apology for Raimond Sebond (trans. Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt)
more:
Michel de Montaigne more or less invented the essay, a word that means ‘attempt’ in French. This line sits inside his longest one, where he pokes holes in human arrogance. We assume animals are dim, but on what evidence? We can’t see inside them any more than they can see inside us.

His motto was ‘What do I know?’

text: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe … the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
author: Immanuel Kant
source: Critique of Practical Reason, Conclusion (trans. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott)
more:
Kant opens the conclusion of the Critique of Practical Reason, his 1788 book on ethics, with this. It’s one of the few lyrical moments from a famously dense writer, and probably his most quoted sentence.

The two wonders mirror each other. The night sky shows how tiny we are, one creature on a speck in a huge universe. The moral law shows how big we are: beings who can act on reason and duty instead of impulse. Kant put human dignity in that second fact.

text: Philosophy is to be studied, not for the sake of any definite answers to its questions … but rather for the sake of the questions themselves…
author: Bertrand Russell
source: The Problems of Philosophy, Chapter 15: The Value of Philosophy (1912)
more:
Bertrand Russell wrote The Problems of Philosophy in 1912 as a short introduction for general readers, and this is from the last chapter. He admits philosophy rarely settles anything. Once a question can be answered for sure, it tends to break off and become its own science.

So why bother? Russell says the questions widen your sense of what’s possible and loosen the grip of prejudices you never chose.

text: When we read, another person thinks for us: we merely repeat his mental process.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: On Reading and Books, in Essays of Schopenhauer (trans. Mrs. Rudolf Dircks)
more:
Arthur Schopenhauer, the 19th-century German philosopher best known for his pessimism, was also sharp about reading. The essay goes on to say that someone who reads all day without stopping to think slowly loses the ability to think for himself, the way a man who always rides forgets how to walk.

A slightly awkward thing to find in a feed of quotes.

text: …all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
em: as difficult as they are rare
author: Baruch Spinoza
source: Ethics, Part 5, Proposition 42, Note (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
more:
These are the last words of Spinoza’s Ethics, a book laid out like geometry, with definitions, axioms and proofs. Spinoza argued that freedom comes from understanding. The more clearly we see the causes of our emotions, the less they push us around.

The closing note admits the path is very hard and few take it. Spinoza lived modestly, earning part of his living grinding lenses, and turned down a professorship at Heidelberg, perhaps to protect his freedom to think.

title: The banality of evil
text: At the trial of Nazi official Adolf Eichmann, Hannah Arendt expected a monster. She found a careerist who spoke in clichés and seemed strangely thoughtless.
em: a careerist who spoke in clichés
author: Hannah Arendt
source: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil (1963)
more:
Arendt went to Jerusalem in 1961 to cover the trial for The New Yorker, and her book caused an uproar. Critics said she was excusing Eichmann. She wasn’t. Her point was that he was frighteningly normal: ambitious, obedient and thoughtless rather than demonic.

That moves where we look for danger. If evil needed monsters, most of us could relax. She argued it can come from ordinary people following orders and chasing promotions without asking what their work actually does.

title: Socrates never wrote a word
text: Socrates wrote nothing at all. Most of what we know about him comes from his students Plato and Xenophon, who wrote about him after his death.
more:
This creates what scholars call the Socratic problem. How much of ‘Socrates’ is the real man, and how much is Plato putting his own ideas in his teacher’s mouth? Plato’s Socrates and Xenophon’s don’t always sound alike, and the comic playwright Aristophanes mocked yet another version on stage.

In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates even voices a suspicion of writing. A text can’t answer back when you question it, and it can look wise without being wise.

title: A lamp in broad daylight
text: Diogenes the Cynic owned almost nothing and slept in a storage jar in Athens. By day he carried a lit lamp, saying he was looking for a human being.
author: Diogenes of Sinope
more:
Diogenes lived in the 4th century BC and treated his whole life as a philosophical performance. If the good life means living by nature, he reasoned, most of what society prizes, like wealth, manners and status, is clutter. Later Roman writers turned his jar into a barrel, which is how he’s usually drawn today.

In the most famous story, Alexander the Great visits and asks if he wants anything. Diogenes tells him to stand a little out of his sun.

title: Descartes and the 5 a.m. lessons
text: In 1649 Descartes agreed to tutor Queen Christina of Sweden three times a week at 5 a.m. He caught pneumonia and died in Stockholm in February 1650.
author: René Descartes
more:
By 1649 Descartes was one of the most famous thinkers in Europe, and Christina invited him to set up a scientific academy and teach her his ideas. It went badly. She rejected his mechanical philosophy, he didn’t share her love of ancient Greek, and by mid-January they’d met only four or five times.

Pneumonia is the standard account of his death. Other causes have been floated over the years, including poisoning theories tied to the religious tensions of the time.

title: The ring of invisibility
text: A ring makes you invisible whenever you like, and nobody would ever know what you did. Would you still act exactly as you do now?
author: Plato
more:
Glaucon, in Plato’s Republic, says nobody would. He tells the story of Gyges, a shepherd who finds a ring of invisibility and uses it to seduce a queen, kill a king and seize the throne. People are only just, he argues, because they fear getting caught.

Much of the rest of the Republic is Socrates’ long reply. Justice, he says, is good for the soul in itself, a kind of inner harmony worth having for its own sake.
